processing: Orthodox tea from the season's first tender leaves, rolled by hand or machine. As with Darjeeling first flush, oxidation is generally kept light, which explains the pale cup.
harvest_season: From around the fourth week of March to the end of April.
appearance_dry: Typically wiry, tender leaf with green tones and tips, though some lots run golden-brown.
appearance_liquor: Light yellowish green, closer to a green tea than to a typical black.
appearance_wet: Tender, bright leaf with a greenish cast, as is usual for spring pickings.
taste_profile: Delicate and fresh, with floral and green herbal notes and a light body.

brewing.notes: General guidance for delicate spring black teas. Use water off the boil and no milk; hot water and long steeps turn it sharp.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year as the spring crop, generally arriving after the April picking ends. It is the costliest flush because little is made and demand exceeds supply. As with other first flush teas, freshness is the point, so buy the current year and finish it within about a year.
description:
Nepal First Flush is the spring picking of the country's orthodox hill tea, mostly from Ilam and nearby eastern districts. It is the lightest, most delicate of the four Nepali flushes, and it often gets compared with a Darjeeling first flush.

The young leaf comes off the Chinese-variety bushes as growth restarts after winter. Tender shoots and a light hand keep a lot of green in the leaf, which is why the cup looks closer to a pale gold than to anything you would call black tea.

In the cup it is floral and fresh with a herbal, grassy edge. Tasting language for it leans on sellers' descriptions, so treat the specifics as a guide. The usual mistake is brewing it like an ordinary black tea: cooler water and shorter steeps treat it better, and it does not want milk.

Look for the year and the garden. Good lots show plenty of tips and a clean, fresh smell; a flat, hay-like smell usually means old stock. Side by side with a Darjeeling first flush of the same year, it makes a nice comparison.
history: Little is documented about this flush in its own right. It belongs to Nepal's orthodox tea, which grew out of the hill estates of Ilam, the first of them set up around 1863, and the four-flush calendar it shares with Darjeeling.
